summary: Louisiana has no law that prohibits keeping a captive-bred roof rat, and the lawful pathway is the same one the fancy rat (the domesticated Norway rat, R. norvegicus) already uses. The state wildlife code (La. R.S. 56:8) sorts wild quadrupeds into game (deer, bears, squirrels, rabbits), outlaw (coyotes, armadillos, feral hogs), protected (wolves, cougars, bobcats, foxes), and nongame (fur/skin animals such as nutria, mink, muskrat); R. rattus fits none. The 'potentially dangerous wild quadruped' ban (LAC 76:V-115) covers only big cats, bears, wolves, and primates, with no rodents. Local 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances (e.g. the Louisiana SPCA code for Orleans Parish) expressly exempt captive-bred 'laboratory rats... which have never known the wild' and the catch-all 'pocket pets or rodents,' which a multi-generation captive-bred roof rat fits. So keeping, hobby breeding, private rehoming, and direct retail sale are effectively legal at the state level. Commercial sale needs no LDWF license: the Nongame Quadruped Breeder/Exhibitor License covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' and federal AWA retail-pet-store sales of rats are exempt from USDA licensing. Parish ordinances vary, and releasing a roof rat is always prohibited (R.S. 56:20).

keep.why: Keeping a captive-bred roof rat needs no Louisiana permit and follows the same route as the fancy rat. R. rattus is on no prohibited or dangerous list: the 'potentially dangerous wild quadruped' rule (LAC 76:V-115) lists only big cats, bears, wolves, and non-human primates, with no rodents, and the wildlife code's enumerated quadruped categories (La. R.S. 56:8: game, outlaw, protected, nongame) do not reach a non-native commensal rodent. Local 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances reinforce this: the Louisiana SPCA code (Orleans Parish) expressly permits 'laboratory rats... which have been bred and raised in captivity which have never known the wild, and pocket pets or rodents including, but not limited to, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chinchillas, sugar gliders or hedgehogs.' A captive-bred roof rat is a rodent and fits the 'pocket pets or rodents' catch-all, identical to the captive-bred Norway rat sold as the fancy rat. Confidence is medium, not high, because R. rattus is nowhere named by species and parish ordinances vary in wording and enforcement.
keep.governing_law: LAC 76:V-115 (potentially dangerous wild quadrupeds; no rodents); La. R.S. 56:8 (game/outlaw/protected/nongame quadruped definitions; R. rattus fits none); local 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances with a 'laboratory rats... pocket pets or rodents' carve-out (e.g. Louisiana SPCA / Orleans Parish).

breed.why: Private hobby breeding of captive-born roof rats triggers no state wildlife license. The Nongame Quadruped Breeder License (La. R.S. 56:262) applies to 'imported or native nongame quadrupeds,' which the wildlife code (R.S. 56:8) defines as fur/skin animals such as alligators, beavers, mink, muskrats, nutrias, and foxes; a non-native commensal rodent with no pelt value falls outside it. LDWF confirms the nongame license covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' and the Game Breeder License (R.S. 56:171) covers wild game species (deer, squirrels, rabbits, game birds), not rodents. The state has no rodent or pocket-pet breeder license, so home breeding for the pet trade sits outside the licensing regime. No-release obligation applies (R.S. 56:20).
breed.governing_law: La. R.S. 56:262 + LDWF Nongame Quadruped Breeder/Exhibitor License (alligators/coyotes/foxes only; not issued for pets or the pet trade); La. R.S. 56:171 (game breeder license; game species only); La. R.S. 56:8 (nongame = fur/skin animals); La. R.S. 56:20 (no-release).

sell_give.why: Both private rehoming and direct retail sale of captive-bred roof rats are unregulated by Louisiana wildlife law. The DR's open question (whether commercial sale needs a Nongame Quadruped Breeder License under R.S. 56:262) resolves against any license: LDWF states that license covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' and R. rattus lacks the fur/skin value the nongame definition (R.S. 56:8) requires. At the federal level, the Animal Welfare Act exempts 'retail pet stores' (a seller and buyer physically present so the buyer can observe the animal before purchase) from USDA licensing, and APHIS lists rats among the species this exemption covers, treating them like dogs, cats, rabbits, guinea pigs, and hamsters. So selling a roof rat face-to-face needs neither a state LDWF license nor a federal USDA license. Only a wholesale/sight-unseen operation (e.g. bulk online or supplying pet-store chains) could trigger USDA APHIS licensing; even then state law stays silent. Parish ordinances may add local limits.
sell_give.governing_law: La. R.S. 56:262 + LDWF Nongame Quadruped Breeder/Exhibitor License (pet trade excluded); La. R.S. 56:8 (nongame quadruped = fur/skin animals; R. rattus excluded); federal Animal Welfare Act retail-pet-store exemption, 9 CFR 1.1 / 2.1 (rats included; USDA license not required for direct retail sale).

transport.why: Intrastate transport of a captive-bred roof rat is unrestricted: a roof rat is not a game quadruped (no transport tags, R.S. 56:125) and not a potentially dangerous wild quadruped (no escape plan or specialized enclosure), so it travels in an ordinary secure pet carrier with no state documentation. For interstate import, Louisiana's animal-health rules (LAC 7:XXI) require a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection and rabies proof for dogs and cats, and govern livestock and poultry, but do not list pet rodents, so the State Veterinarian requires no CVI, permit, or entry report for a privately owned pet rat crossing state lines. International import is governed federally by the CDC: the African rodent ban (42 CFR 71.56) reaches only rodents of African origin or African native habitat, and R. rattus is native to Asia, so it is not barred by that rule. Practical caveats not set by state law: commercial airlines/pet shippers often demand a recent health certificate as a private policy, and never release the animal (R.S. 56:20).
transport.governing_law: La. R.S. 56:125 (game-quadruped transport tags; N/A to rodents); LAC 76:V-115 (dangerous-quadruped travel rules; N/A); LAC 7:XXI (LDAF import health rules; dogs/cats/livestock only, no pet-rodent CVI); 42 CFR 71.56 (CDC African rodent ban; Asian-origin R. rattus not covered); La. R.S. 56:20 (no-release).

restrictions.summary: No Louisiana wildlife license applies to breeding or selling captive-bred pet roof rats. The Nongame Quadruped Breeder/Exhibitor License (La. R.S. 56:262) covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade'; R. rattus is not a fur/skin nongame quadruped. The state has no rodent or pocket-pet breeder license. Federally, direct retail sale of rats is exempt from USDA licensing under the AWA retail-pet-store exemption; only wholesale/sight-unseen sale could trigger a USDA APHIS license.
steps: No state license needed for hobby breeding or face-to-face sale of captive-bred roof rats
If operating wholesale or selling sight-unseen at scale, check USDA APHIS dealer-license rules under the Animal Welfare Act
restrictions.where_to_file: Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries (Wildlife Permits) for any state question; USDA APHIS Animal Care for wholesale federal licensing
restrictions.fees: No applicable state fee for pet rats

restrictions.summary: Never release a roof rat into the wild. R.S. 56:20 forbids liberating any pen-raised or wild animal within the state without written permission of the LDWF secretary; a violation is a class four offense (R.S. 56:34). The roof rat is treated as an unprotected invasive pest the moment it is outside a cage. Keep it indoors in a secure enclosure.
steps: Keep roof rats indoors in secure, escape-proof enclosures
Never release, abandon, or rehome a roof rat into the wild (R.S. 56:20, class four violation)

restrictions.summary: Parish and municipal 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances vary. Many (e.g. the Louisiana SPCA code for Orleans Parish) expressly exempt captive-bred 'laboratory rats' and 'pocket pets or rodents,' which a captive-bred roof rat fits, but enforcement of the exact species can vary by parish and officer. Check your own parish/city code before keeping or selling.
steps: Read your parish/municipal animal-control ordinance for any 'wild or exotic animal' rule and its pocket-pet/rodent exemption
restrictions.where_to_file: Local parish or municipal animal control

inquiry_focus: Primary state question (LDWF): does LDWF classify a captive-bred Rattus rattus kept and bred purely as a pet as a 'wild quadruped' or 'nongame quadruped' under La. R.S. 56:8, and does breeding or commercial retail sale require a Game Breeder (R.S. 56:171) or Nongame Quadruped Breeder (R.S. 56:262) license? The LDWF licensing page states the nongame license covers only alligators/coyotes/foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' so the expected answer is no license; a written confirmation would close the only state-law gap. Secondary question (LDAF State Veterinarian): does Louisiana require a CVI, import permit, or 10-day report to bring a captive-bred pet rat in from another state (LAC 7:XXI lists no pet-rodent rule)?
